a3420.t:
Pingyang county in east China’s Zhejiang province, has reinvented itself as a pet-lover’s paradise. When 1990s-born local Zeng Yao invites fellow enthusiasts to his hometown, he offers a mix of business and leisure: “Spend a weekend dressing up your dog for our pet fashion show. Browse our pet supply superstore. Tour the pet food factory right next door.”
Nestled between verdant mountains and the Aojiang River, Pingyang is known for its picturesque landscapes. Today, however, its identity is equally shaped by an omnipresent pet culture – from countryside homestays offering cozy dog houses and eco-friendly cat litter to urban streets adorned with whimsical pet-themed murals.
This identity marks a deliberate transformation. Two decades ago, Pingyang thrived as a leather-processing hub, home to over 1,200 tanneries at its peak. While lucrative, the industry exacted an environmental toll, spurring a shift in the local economy.
“In the 1990s, traders arrived seeking discarded pig and cow hides. None of us imagined those scraps would become premium pet chews!” recalled Chen Zhenbiao, a resident of Shuitou township in Pingyang. Sensing a business opportunity, he founded Peidi Animal Nutrition Technology Co., Ltd., a producer of high-protein pet goods.
Today, Shuitou’s Chongle Road showcases the industry’s scale: two publicly listed pet supply companies stand opposite each other, distributing products worldwide. In 2024 alone, nearly 100 pet enterprises in Pingyang generated over 5 billion yuan (697.81 million) in output. The county now accounts for more than half of China’s pet chew exports and a third of the country’s pet leash production.
Inside Peidi’s production workshop, workers slice duck, chicken, and beef before freeze-drying – a process that produces gourmet pet snacks. “Consumers increasingly seek trusted brands and specialized products, creating a vast, segmented market,” said the company’s deputy general manager Tang Zhaobo. Beyond chews, Peidi now produces pet food, meat snacks, and even pet-friendly ice cream.
Zeng Yao, leveraging Shuitou’s leather-making legacy, developed transparent, portable pet crates after years of experience in the luggage industry. Nearby in Wanquan township, manufacturers have shifted from household furnishings to pet sofas and scratching boards. With government support, such adaptations have expanded Pingyang’s pet sector into dozens of categories spanning food, toys, apparel, and accessories.
Yet product diversification alone cannot guarantee success. The real challenge lies in breaking into the market. “Historically reliant on exports, we’ve shifted focus to China’s booming domestic market,” Zeng explained.
To capture this demand, Pingyang unveiled a flagship experiential hub: Pet Town. The sprawling complex showcases local and national brands, allowing visitors to explore curated selections of pet products.
Adjacent to it, a newly launched livestreaming center hums with activity. “This hybrid model blending livestream e-commerce, tourism, and retail drives brand visibility and cultivates influencers. Over 50 local pet brands now broadcast from the facility,” said Zeng, who also runs a digital development company and a storefront on Chinese e-commerce platform JD.com.
Zeng Xinyi runs a livestream channel where she often chats enthusiastically with viewers. A graduate of a pet care program at a vocational school in Pingyang, she chose to remain in her hometown after finishing her studies. The school offers several pet-related majors, and thanks to partnerships with local companies, many graduates find jobs quickly in the thriving local sector.
True to its name, Pet Town integrates animals into its core experience. Themed events – from brand exhibitions to pet contests and curated travel itineraries for pet owners – merge tourism with commerce along Pingyang’s scenic landscapes. Streets once silent now pulse with the energy of visitors and their companions.
“We’re developing comprehensive pet-inclusive tourism: accredited boarding, pet-friendly campgrounds, dedicated buses, hotels, and self-service grooming stations. Our goal is to become a premier destination for pet lovers,” said an official from the county’s culture, media, tourism and sports bureau.
“This is a big business,” said Zeng. He plans to replicate the Pet Town concept nationally, hoping more people will get to know Pingyang through its vibrant pet industry.

a3684.t:
ABUJA – The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Barr. Nyesom Wike, on Thursday issued a bold charge to African leaders and investors to abandon the continent’s longstanding reliance on foreign aid and take full responsibility for shaping its economic future.
Speaking while delivering the keynote address at the 2025 Innovate Africa Conference held at the ECOWAS Conference Hall, Abuja, Wike insisted that Africa’s development lies not in donor funding but in visionary leadership, home-grown investment, and renewed confidence in its people.
“Africa must now rise above aid, rediscover her strength, and rebuild her institutions,” Wike declared. “Development cannot be donated; it must be built. Our future must be crafted not in the conference rooms of donor agencies, but in the creative laboratories, farms, classrooms, and workshops of Africans determined to transform their continent.”
The event, convened by Innovate Africa Corporation, brought together African leaders, global partners, business executives, investors, academics, and innovators to reimagine leadership and economic transformation across the continent.
Wike, who was honored with the Innovate Africa Leadership Award 2025, dedicated the recognition to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the Nigerian people, saying it underscored Abuja’s ongoing infrastructural renewal and governance reforms.
“This honour belongs not to me alone, but to the resilient people of Nigeria, and especially to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, whose bold vision for renewal has given me the platform to contribute to our nation’s transformation,” he said.
The Minister expressed concern that despite Africa’s youth population and abundant natural wealth, progress remains stifled by weak institutions, unemployment, and failed governance systems.
“How can a continent so richly blessed remain so constrained?” he questioned. “Leadership remains the fulcrum upon which the destinies of nations turn.”
Wike called for a shift from transactional to transformational leadership, emphasizing humility, service, accountability, and difficult policy choices.
He praised President Tinubu’s early reforms especially fuel subsidy removal and decentralization efforts as an example of leadership that “dares where others hesitate.”
“If we can reimagine leadership across Africa in this same spirit leadership that builds, not blames; that inspires, not divides then no mountain will be too high, and no dream too ambitious for our continent,” he added.
Wike highlighted that 70% of Africans are under 30, describing the demographic as “a revolution waiting to happen.”
“The energy, creativity, and resilience of Africa’s young population are not just assets; they are the very instruments of the continent’s transformation,” he said, urging increased investment in education, digital literacy, innovation, and entrepreneurship.
He stressed that infrastructure must serve as an “equalizer,” connecting talent to opportunity and unlocking productivity on a continental scale.
Referencing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), Wike noted that regional integration remains Africa’s clearest path to prosperity.
“The AfCFTA is a declaration of intent that Africa will no longer accept to be a supplier of raw materials and a dumping ground for finished goods,” he stated.
“It is the cornerstone of Africa’s second liberation the liberation of its economy.”
Closing his remarks, Wike challenged African leaders, investors, and citizens to stop waiting for external deliverance and assume full ownership of the continent’s destiny.
“History will not remember what we merely dreamed for Africa; it will remember what we did for Africa,” he said.
“The future will not be given to us. We must build it. And we must build it now.”
He expressed hope that the ideas shared at the conference would inspire concrete steps toward making Africa “a land of fulfillment, dignity, and shared prosperity.”
Earlier in his remarks, the Chairman of the occasion, Mazi Sam Ohuabunwa, lamented that Africa continues to struggle under the weight of incompetent leadership and political systems designed to keep a few in power at the expense of national progress.
He warned that many political leaders in the continent attain leadership “by all means” and then build structures to perpetuate themselves or their families in government, rather than delivering development for citizens.
He said Africa must undergo what he called a “leadership metamorphosis” a deliberate transformation that will unlock the continent’s economic potential, strengthen competitiveness, and accelerate sustainable development.
According to him, such a shift will drive economic growth, improve living standards, and attract long-term investment that is not tied to election cycles or foreign dictates.
Outlining the priorities for Africa’s future, Ohuabunwa urged leaders to adopt Africa-led solutions, embrace inclusive and sustainable growth, and promote inter-country cooperation that breaks down outdated boundaries.
He stressed the need for political systems that allow every citizen including the youth and those with “silent talent” to participate meaningfully in national development. He emphasized that Africa must shift “from aid to partnerships” that genuinely serve the continent’s interests.
The former Presidential aspirant further listed key leadership competencies required for Africa’s transformation, including sound and digital education, innovation capacity, effective communication, emotional intelligence, integrity, accountability, and the ability to translate ideas into action. “Leadership is not for bullies or daydreamers,” Ohuabunwa declared.
“We need leaders who can make sacrifices, keep their promises, and deliver results in the national interest not personal gain.”

a3817.t:
As Malawi approaches its September 2025 general elections, political manifestos are once again filled with promises of infrastructure, education, and job creation. Yet, one critical pillar of economic transformation is conspicuously absent: banking reform. Specifically, the urgent need to expand the number of banks across the country. I haven’t seen pledges to set up national, regional and district investments banks across the country.
Malawi, one of the poorest nations in the world, doesn’t just need better banks— it needs more banks. And this is not just a matter of convenience; it’s a matter of urgent economic survival.
Drawing on the work of Richard Werner, a world-renowned economist known for his theory of credit creation, we begin to understand why banking is not merely a service but a powerful engine of economic development. Werner argues that banks are not intermediaries that lend out deposits, as commonly believed.
Instead, banks create money through the process of credit creation. When a bank issues a loan, it simultaneously creates a deposit in the borrower’s account— effectively generating new money. This means that banks have the unique ability to expand the money supply and stimulate economic activity, especially when credit is directed toward productive sectors like small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
In Malawi, however, this engine is sputtering. The country has fewer than a dozen commercial banks serving a population of over 20 million. Most of these banks are concentrated in urban centres, leaving rural districts underserved and unbanked. According to the Reserve Bank of Malawi, only about 30% of Malawians have access to formal banking services. This leaves the majority of citizens—especially small business owners, farmers, and informal traders—without access to the credit they need to grow their enterprises.
- Advertisement -
The big banks that dominate Malawi’s financial landscape are often risk-averse and profit-driven, focusing on large corporate clients and government bonds. They rarely extend credit to small businesses in districts like Chitipa, Nsanje, or Ntcheu. The result is a financial system that excludes the very entrepreneurs who could drive local development and job creation.
Imagine a different model: one where each district in Malawi has at least three banks, or at least an investment bank of its own, tailored to the specific needs of local businesses. A bank in Mzimba might specialise in agricultural finance, offering loans for irrigation and livestock. A bank in Mangochi could focus on tourism-related enterprises, while one in Zomba might support educational startups and tech hubs. These district-level banks would be closer to the people, more responsive to local conditions, and better positioned to channel credit into productive uses.
This decentralised banking model is not a fantasy. It’s a proven strategy in countries like Germany and China. In fact, China’s economic miracle over the past four decades was made possible in large part by the aggressive expansion of its banking sector. The Chinese government licensed thousands of local banks and credit cooperatives, which flooded the economy with credit targeted at SMEs, infrastructure, and manufacturing. Today, China leads the world in banking assets and has one of the most extensive banking networks globally.
According to World Bank data, countries like Germany and France have over 30 commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, while Malawi lags far behind. This disparity is not just statistical— it’s structural. It reflects the difference between economies that empower their citizens with access to finance and those that leave them behind.
- Advertisement -
- Advertisement -
The political implications are profound. If Malawi is serious about creating millions of jobs, it must empower its SMEs. And SMEs cannot thrive without access to capital. This is where political parties must step up. Instead of vague promises about job creation, they should commit to banking reform that includes licensing more banks, encouraging district-level financial institutions, and ensuring that credit flows to the productive sectors of the economy.
Moreover, expanding the banking sector would have ripple effects across society. It would increase financial inclusion, reduce poverty, and stimulate innovation. It would also enhance the resilience of local economies, making them less dependent on foreign aid and more capable of self-sustained growth.
As we look ahead to the elections, it’s time for political leaders to recognise that banking is not just a technical issue—it’s a strategic lever for national development. The current number of banks is woefully inadequate for a country with Malawi’s aspirations. We need a bold vision that sees banking as a tool for empowerment, not just profit.
For Malawi to rise, we must bank the unbanked, finance the unfunded, and support the unseen entrepreneurs in every district. The road to prosperity runs through the doors of local banks. Let’s build them.

a4047.t:
More than 20 African countries are either already facing debt distress or on the brink, Claver Gatete, Executive secretary of United Nations Economic commission for Africa (UNECA) said on Monday.
Gatete made the remark during the inaugural of the African Union Debt Conference, Lomé, capital of Togo, under the theme: “Africa’s public debt management agenda in restoring and safeguarding debt sustainability.”
In his speech seen by APA, Gatete said in 2024, Africa’s total public debt shot up to US$1.86 trillion, with average debt-to-GDP ratios rising from 44.4% in 2015 to 66.7% today.
When debt repayments outweigh investments in health and education combined, we must question the sustainability and human cost of our fiscal path.
He said across Africa, access to concessional finance is narrowing, while tariff escalations are weakening market access for African goods.
Accordingly, the executive secretary said many African countries are facing higher borrowing costs, reduced export revenues and tighter budgets, at a time when fiscal expansion is essential for inclusive growth.
“Africa is not merely confronting a debt crisis; it is facing a development crisis – one where debt servicing competes directly with health, education, infrastructure and the fundamental right to development,” Gatete said.
He said the international financial lifelines Africa once relied on, including Official Development Assistance, are fading.
According to the executive secretary, today, 83 percent of USAID programmes have been cancelled and traditional partners are tightening their budgets.
Gatete went on saying the cost of capital has surged, and the G20 Common Framework, unfortunately, remains slow, opaque and creditor-biased.
MG/abj/APA

a4074.t:
Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority’s Executive Director Dr. Luke Bawo has outlined progress made by his organization during the past five months, highlighting several key initiatives.
He said though significant strides have been made in safeguarding public health in Liberia, he acknowledged that challenges still remain.
Appearing at the Ministry of Information Culture and Tourism (MICAT) regular press briefing last week, Dr. Bawo noted that the organization has been active in seven counties and is focusing on the waste management of health products.
He also said the LMHRA has undergone staff restructuring to enhance operational efficiency and has made strides in de-escalating tensions within the organization to foster a culture of inclusiveness.
Regulatory frameworks surrounding narcotics and psychotropic substances have been effectively migrated from the Ministry of Health to the LMHRA, reinforcing its authority in this sector, he disclosed.
A press release issued by LMHRA quotes him as indicating that the Construction of a new laboratory is underway, which is vital for the organization’s capacity to effectively assess and regulate health products.
The LMHRA boss also mentioned significant achievements, including the formation of a reappointed Hearing Board designed to offer impartial reviews of alleged violations in health product regulations.
An assessment has started in Maryland County to establish the LMHRA’s Region-4 office, demonstrating the regulatory authority’s commitment to decentralization and increased coverage, the release further quoted Dr. Bawo as stating.
However, he did not shy away from discussing the challenges facing the LMHRA, particularly highlighting issues such as system clogs due to expired products in circulation that pose risks to public health; the rising issue of street peddling of medicines; the lack of adherence to donation regulations, leading to inefficiencies within the supply chain and the need for laboratory system strengthening and enhanced technological support to manage regulations effectively.
Despite these hindrances, Dr. Bawo says his organization remains optimistic, emphasizing the need for collaborative efforts of key stakeholders such as the Ministry of Health, WHO, USAID, and other partners in striving to achieve WHO maturity level 3 and ISO 17025 accreditation for LMHRA’s laboratory.
He reaffirmed the commitment of the LMHRA to ensuring that Liberians have access to safe, effective, and high-quality medicines, underscoring the regulatory authority’s vital role in public health and safety.
He earlier expressed his gratitude to both MICAT for the opportunity given him and to His Excellency Joseph N. Boakai for the opportunity to lead the LMHRA.
“The maintenance of good health is paramount to nation-building,” Dr. Bawo stated, articulating the broader implications of health on the nation’s quality of life.
He pointed out the psychological burdens faced by families coping with poor health, which can lead to catastrophic financial consequences.
He added: “The health sector is making strides in improving diagnostic services, detecting diseases, and instituting curative and rehabilitative measures. However, protection of the health of the population extends beyond diagnosis and treatment; it involves ensuring that medicines and health products are of the highest quality
Dr. Bawo underscored various critical public health issues, referencing alarming international incidents, such as the tragic case of contaminated cough syrup in The Gambia, which resulted in the deaths of about 70 children.
He expressed concerns regarding the prevalence of falsified medicines and improper dosages in the marketplace, asking key questions about the quality and safety of medications that citizens rely on daily.
The LMHRA was established by an act of law in 2010, with a clear mandate: to ensure that safe, effective, and quality medicines are available to the Liberian public. Its objectives include protecting the public from harmful products, ensuring fair trade practices, combating illegal trade, and promoting pharmacovigilance through research and timely dissemination of drug information.

a4267.t:
Today, the illegal artisanal mining, called galamsey, has become a menace, an existential threat to the Republic of Ghana.
What started as a source of livelihood for many young Ghanaians, and an income stream for the Government, has become a scar on the conscience of the highest echelons of political leadership due to the devastated impacts it has had on human lives, health and environmental resources.
One may ask, why are we here? In the 1990s the quest for diversifying the Ghanaian economy to broaden its income stream saw the enactment of legal instruments for issuing licenses for artisanal miners to engage in small scale mining operations.
The artisanal miners were to exist side by side with large scale mining concessioners; in some cases feeding off from ‘old’ concessions.
Operating under a controlled environment, subscribing to rule of laws, respecting concession boundaries, managing environmental impacts and operating within the confines of the social requirements of communities of operations, artisanal mining became one of the surest way to boost small scale and medium enterprises within the natural resources sector. A very lucrative but fine businesses then.
Artisanal
Artisanal mining became something else when it metamorphosed its name to ‘Galamsey’, following the involvement of political stalwarts and high cash handed Chinese businessmen and women who came in with funds and capacity for massive extraction of minerals symptomatic of pillaging.
The galamseyers targeted all possible sources of gold- forest estates, cocoa farms, agricultural farmsteads, watersheds and river sources.
By 2016, the supply chains on the market had become extremely sophisticated with players that are untouchable.
The players include powerful licensed agents and issuers, highly connected politicians, wealthy Chinese businessmen, mayors, parliamentarians, community elders, members of the security sector and some traditional chiefs.
To the extent that even the pronouncements of the  President of the Republic that he was placing his presidency on the line marshaling the security forces as the commander in chief of the armed forces did not deter the players of the supply chain.
 
Today, galamsey has gravely destroyed all of our major rivers that supply fishery and water resources to over 15 million population of Ghanaians.
Especially rivers pra and offin have attained toxic levels too dangerous for consumption by WHO standards.
These rivers contains metalloids, such as lead, cadmium, copper, arsenic, mercury, iron, and zinc, making it unsuitable for domestic use.
The tributaries of these rivers have carried these pollutants all over the country affecting river streams in several regions including now Greater Accra region.
As a result Ghana is facing significant challenges related to access to clean water. About 25 per cent of the population lacks access to clean water, and the country is moving towards water stress.
In addition to diminishing water access, the health impacts of galamsey is dreadful. Some of the physical health impacts are (i) Mercury poisoning, including exposure to mercury used in gold extraction causes neurological damage, kidney damage, and birth defects; (ii) heavy metal contamination. Lead, arsenic, and cadmium in water and soil cause various health issues, including cancer, respiratory problems, and organ damage; (iii) Waterborne diseases. Polluted water sources lead to increased risk of cholera, typhoid, and diarrhoea; (iv) Respiratory problems.
Dust and chemical exposure cause respiratory issues, such as silicosis and bronchitis.
With soils contaminated by toxic metals, Ghana will be threatened by food insecurity.
Already the country has not recovered from post COVID food production impacts as well as recent effects of climate variability.
Recent evidence of heavy metal presence in cocoa beans and food products such as yams and cassava points to the looming grave consequences of staples shortages for the country.
In essence, what are citizens going to do? Are we going to rely hundred percent on food imports? This is a possibility with serious ramifications for foreign exchange and the ever depreciating cedi currency.
Impact
Further, the impact on environmental resources cannot be overstated. Contaminated river bodies and soils meant that a wide spectrum of biodiversity would have been destroyed.
These may include food chains and habitats of rare, endangered and indigenous species of all categories.
Destruction of forest estates would have devastating effects on high conservation value species and the utter destruction of Ghana’s genetic heat indices.
Some of the forest estates might become so destroyed beyond reparations and recovery, affecting Ghana’s overall contribution to climate action and preservation of global biodiversity.
How can we solve the galamsey problem once and for all? I propose a number of ways, including bold policy options and punitive measures, to deter reoccurrence.
The solutions are set out as follows. Firstly, ban artisanal/galamsey mining indefinitely.
This will allow for time to review it’s licensing schemes, analyse additional requirements to to safeguard impacts of activities on environmental resources.
The ban will also help to review the players to be allowed to engage in the scheme in the future as well as what equipments to allow for the mining activities.
It is proposed that future licensing should prohibit the use of excavators and other sophisticated equipments.
Also non Ghanaian players especially, Chinese must not be permitted to engage the trade.
Secondly, name and shame all political players, including members of Parliament currently seeking re-election in the current electoral processes.
It is proposed that such MPs or politicians must be completely banned from engaging in future politics, even if they get re-elected.
This punitive measure is important to deter such irresponsible behaviour of any category of political leaders.
Thirdly, there must be a robust analysis of beneficiaries of the value and supply chains of the traded Galamsey gold to force the return of at least 80 per cent of some of the moneys to be put in a trust fund for use to correct the impacts.
The value and supply chain participants must be liable to jail-able offences under the country’s rules of law.
A strong case could be made for criminal acts involving willful destruction of nation’s environmental resources as well as causing wanton health problems to a significant Ghanaian population akin to population decimation. Pursuing this case will make Ghana look serious.
Fourthly, engage a rapid assessment of the extent of damage to environmental resources, including effects on human health and production systems in order to design an imminent programme for redress.
The analysis should include the extent of coverage including geospatial distribution of farmlands and communities affected by the crisis.
Once the special distribution is determined, this information must be made available publicly with a command to totally stop any food production from these regions.
Essentially, there must be a seclusion of agriculture foods including inland fisheries from the local food distribution supply chain. This ban must be enforced until such time as the environment is cleaned.
Science and technology
Lastly, engage science and technology solution for cleaning the water sources, decontamination of soils and restoring the ecological integrity of our ecosystems.
The technological solution exists to destroy the man-made chemicals (per-fluorinate substances-PFAs) and the metalloids to clean the waters and soils of these substances.
But the exercise is very expensive and could cost several billions of dollars to do so. However, the good news is that the solution and expertise exist that we can tap into.
Besides, the cleaning process would engage human capacities which would create jobs for Ghanaians, including some of those who have engaged in the Galamsey in the first place.
With the above commonsensical solutions, I believe that we will be able to deal effectively with the prevailing Galamsey situation addressing its existential threats to the nation.
The writer is a former senior UN diplomat, a strategic advisor to governments and development partners

a4312.t:
Mozambique will continue to have access to HIV/AIDS treatment funded by the United States of America (USA). The announcement comes after the revocation of the US executive order announcing the suspension of foreign development assistance for ninety days, to assess programmatic efficiency and alignment with the US government’s foreign policy.
Last Thursday, the US government approved an “emergency humanitarian waiver” that authorizes the immediate resumption of mother-to-child HIV treatment and prevention services.
According to a note from the US State Department, the measure is supported by the US President’s Emergency Plan for HIV/AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) – the largest global initiative to respond to the disease.
The approval of the “emergency humanitarian waiver” represents a retreat by the US administration in the face of global pressure for the United States of America to continue funding the global response to HIV in order to achieve the common goal of ending the pandemic.

a4331.t:
Le Sofitel Hôtel de Cotonou a accueilli ce 08 mai 2025, la dixième édition de l’Africa SME Champions Forum. La rencontre est qualifiée de conclave stratégique et réunit les acteurs clés de l’écosystème entrepreneurial africain. Leur rôle à ce forum est de redéfinir les voies de croissance des petites et moyennes entreprises (PME) sur le continent.
Depuis 10 ans, AfricSearch group, sous la direction de Didier Acouetey, parcourt l’Afrique, à la rencontre des acteurs des écosystèmes entrepreneuriaux. L’objectif est de faire des PME le socle d’un développement économique durable. L’édition 2025, qui se tient à Cotonou, marque un tournant important. Le forum change son format habituel pour un conclave stratégique. Des différentes réflexions sortiront des recommandations concrètes en vue d’un Pacte de soutien aux PME africaines courant 2025-2035.
Un écosystème à repenser
A l’ouverture du forum les différents intervenants s’accordent sur un constat sans appel : malgré les efforts déployés ces dernières années, les PME africaines peinent toujours à accéder au financement, à l’innovation, et à l’échelle nécessaire pour leur pérennité. “Sur 30 PME accompagnées, aucune n’est encore cotée”, a relevé Félix Amenounve, Directeur général de la Bourse régionale des valeurs mobilières (BRVM).
D’où la nécessité de réinventer les instruments de financement et d’encourager des modèles audacieux qui ont prouvé leur efficacité. Le forum propose ainsi la structuration de “piliers” sectoriels, pour coordonner les banques commerciales, les fonds de garantie, les plateformes digitales, et les marchés financiers autour d’objectifs communs.
L’université comme vivier d’entrepreneurs
Parmi les propositions marquantes, figure la création d’une nouvelle génération de PME issues des universités africaines. Ce modèle s’inspire des succès des entreprises comme Google ou Apple qui sont nées en milieu universitaire aux États-Unis. “L’Afrique doit encourager la naissance de ses géants dans les salles de classe”, a déclaré Félix Amenounve.
L’État en facilitateur, pas en employeur
Le ministre d’État béninois chargé du Plan, Abdoulaye Bio Tchané, a insisté sur la responsabilité des États. Selon lui, “l’État ne peut être le principal pourvoyeur d’emplois”. Il doit plutôt garantir une stabilité macroéconomique, améliorer les infrastructures (notamment l’accès à l’électricité et à internet), et simplifier la vie des entrepreneurs. Il a souligné que “plus de 90 % des entreprises au Bénin sont des PME, mais trop peu passent à l’échelle”.
Les organisateurs du forum espèrent sortir du conclave avec une feuille de route opérationnelle, des engagements fermes, et un nouvel élan collectif pour transformer les défis structurels des PME en opportunités durables.
a4331.en:
The Sofitel Hotel in Cotonou hosted the tenth edition of the Africa SME Champions Forum on 8 May 2025. The meeting is described as a strategic conclave and brings together the key players of the African entrepreneurial ecosystem. Their role at this forum is to redefine the growth paths of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) on the continent.

For 10 years, the AfricSearch group, under the leadership of Didier Acouetey, has travelled across Africa meeting the players of entrepreneurial ecosystems. The objective is to make SMEs the foundation of sustainable economic development. The 2025 edition, held in Cotonou, marks an important turning point. The forum is changing its usual format for a strategic conclave. The various discussions will produce concrete recommendations with a view to a Pact of support for African SMEs over 2025-2035.

An ecosystem to be rethought

At the opening of the forum, the various speakers agreed on an unsparing assessment: despite the efforts made in recent years, African SMEs still struggle to access financing, innovation, and the scale needed for their durability. "Out of 30 SMEs supported, not one is yet listed," noted Felix Amenounve, Director General of the Regional Securities Exchange (BRVM).

Hence the need to reinvent financing instruments and to encourage bold models that have proven their effectiveness. The forum thus proposes structuring sectoral "pillars" to coordinate commercial banks, guarantee funds, digital platforms and financial markets around common objectives.

The university as a breeding ground for entrepreneurs

Among the notable proposals is the creation of a new generation of SMEs emerging from African universities. This model draws on the success of companies such as Google or Apple, which were born in university settings in the United States. "Africa must encourage the birth of its giants in the classroom," declared Felix Amenounve.

The State as facilitator, not employer

Benin's Minister of State in charge of Planning, Abdoulaye Bio Tchane, insisted on the responsibility of States. According to him, "the State cannot be the main provider of jobs." It must instead guarantee macroeconomic stability, improve infrastructure (in particular access to electricity and the internet), and simplify the lives of entrepreneurs. He stressed that "more than 90% of companies in Benin are SMEs, but too few scale up."

The forum's organisers hope to emerge from the conclave with an operational roadmap, firm commitments, and new collective momentum to turn the structural challenges of SMEs into lasting opportunities.

a4415.t:
Sahel et les défis : Le réseau "Elles du Sahel" plaide pour un financement accru
Le mercredi 28 mai 2025, le réseau "Elles du Sahel" a organisé une table ronde afin de restituer les recommandations issues des rencontres tenues l’année précédente.
L’une des principales revendications formulées lors de cet échange est la nécessité d’accroître le financement pour faire face aux défis du Sahel.
Le Sahel, vaste région s’étendant du Sénégal à l’Érythrée, est confronté à une crise profonde aux multiples facettes : l’insécurité croissante, alimentée par les conflits et les groupes armés, la crise alimentaire, avec plus de 5,4 millions de personnes en situation de précarité et 2,8 millions d’enfants souffrant de malnutrition aiguë selon les chiffres des ONG humanitaires.
Il y a également l’instabilité politique, marquée par des Transitions difficiles et des tensions régionales, la crise climatique, qui accentue la désertification et fragilise les communautés et l’urgence humanitaire, qui laisse des millions de personnes en détresse, notamment 2,5 millions de déplacés internes, dont 1,9 million au Burkina Faso.
L’un des aspects préoccupants reste le retrait progressif des bailleurs internationaux, dont l’Usaid en 2025. Cette réduction des financements crée une incertitude croissante quant à la continuité des soutiens nécessaires dans les secteurs clés.
Dans ce contexte, le réseau "Elles du Sahel", composé de 16 femmes originaires du Sahel, de l’Union européenne et des États-Unis, a organisé en 2024 une série de six tables rondes au Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Tchad et Mauritanie, ainsi qu’en Belgique. Ces rencontres ont rassemblé 180 participants issus de 150 organisations, principalement des associations de la société civile locale, avec pour objectif d’amplifier la voix des femmes et des filles face aux défis qu’elles rencontrent.
Ces échanges ont mis en évidence l’urgence de maintenir les investissements en faveur des femmes et des filles, notamment dans des secteurs stratégiques tels que l’éducation, la santé et la justice de genre.
Le rapport intitulé "écoutez les voix du Sahel", synthétisant les principales recommandations, a été présenté aux bailleurs internationaux à Bruxelles.
Lors de la table ronde du 28 mai 2025 de Bamako, une dizaine d’associations féminines et autres acteurs ont pris part aux discussions afin de renforcer le dialogue multipartite et engager les parties prenantes nationales et régionales autour de solutions concrètes pour maintenir et accroître l’aide du financement au Sahel.
Investir au-delà des enjeux sécuritaires
Selon Maïmouna Dioncounda Dembélé, membre fondatrice des "Elles du Sahel", dans un contexte de crise prolongée, les organisations féminines, la société civile et les États doivent investir dans des domaines cruciaux, au-delà des questions de sécurité et de défense.
"Aujourd’hui, nous devons investir davantage dans la santé et l’éducation, des secteurs souvent négligés, notamment en ce qui concerne les problématiques spécifiques au genre. Une de nos recommandations majeures est d’augmenter les financements pour les questions de genre, dans un Sahel fragilisé par le terrorisme", plaide Mme Dioncounda, insistant sur la nécessité de réponses transnationales face aux enjeux transnationaux.
À l’issue de cette rencontre, le réseau "Elles du Sahel" a réitéré son appel pressant à la communauté internationale afin de garantir la participation active des femmes et des filles dans les efforts de paix, de sécurité et de développement au Sahel.
Alors que la région fait face à des défis de plus en plus complexes, l’augmentation du financement apparaît comme une nécessité absolue pour assurer une réponse efficace et durable aux crises qui frappent le Sahel.
Ousmane Mahamane
a4415.en:
The Sahel and its challenges: the "Elles du Sahel" network calls for increased funding

The Sahel and its challenges: the "Elles du Sahel" (Women of the Sahel) network calls for increased funding

On Wednesday 28 May 2025, the "Elles du Sahel" network organised a round table in order to present the recommendations arising from the meetings held the previous year.

One of the main demands formulated during this exchange is the need to increase funding to face the challenges of the Sahel.

The Sahel, a vast region stretching from Senegal to Eritrea, is confronted with a deep, multifaceted crisis: growing insecurity, fuelled by conflicts and armed groups; the food crisis, with more than 5.4 million people in a precarious situation and 2.8 million children suffering from acute malnutrition according to the figures of humanitarian NGOs.

There is also political instability, marked by difficult transitions and regional tensions; the climate crisis, which accentuates desertification and weakens communities; and the humanitarian emergency, which leaves millions of people in distress, notably 2.5 million internally displaced persons, of whom 1.9 million are in Burkina Faso.

One of the worrying aspects remains the progressive withdrawal of international donors, including USAID in 2025. This reduction in funding creates growing uncertainty as to the continuity of the support needed in key sectors.

In this context, the "Elles du Sahel" network, made up of 16 women from the Sahel, the European Union and the United States, organised in 2024 a series of six round tables in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad and Mauritania, as well as in Belgium. These meetings brought together 180 participants from 150 organisations, mainly local civil society associations, with the objective of amplifying the voice of women and girls in the face of the challenges they encounter.

These exchanges highlighted the urgency of maintaining investment in favour of women and girls, notably in strategic sectors such as education, health and gender justice.

The report entitled "Listen to the voices of the Sahel", synthesising the main recommendations, was presented to international donors in Brussels.

At the round table of 28 May 2025 in Bamako, about ten women's associations and other actors took part in the discussions in order to strengthen multi-stakeholder dialogue and engage national and regional stakeholders around concrete solutions to maintain and increase funding aid to the Sahel.

Investing beyond security concerns

According to Maimouna Dioncounda Dembele, founding member of "Elles du Sahel", in a context of prolonged crisis, women's organisations, civil society and states must invest in crucial areas, beyond questions of security and defence.

"Today, we must invest more in health and education, sectors that are often neglected, notably as regards gender-specific issues. One of our major recommendations is to increase funding for gender issues, in a Sahel weakened by terrorism," Mrs Dioncounda pleads, insisting on the need for transnational responses to transnational challenges.

At the end of this meeting, the "Elles du Sahel" network reiterated its urgent appeal to the international community in order to guarantee the active participation of women and girls in the efforts for peace, security and development in the Sahel.

While the region faces increasingly complex challenges, increased funding appears to be an absolute necessity to ensure an effective and sustainable response to the crises striking the Sahel.

Ousmane Mahamane

a4483.t:
Monsieur le Gouverneur, le CNSP a deux ans au pouvoir, quel est l’état général de votre entité administrative en particulier sur le plan sécuritaire ?
«Depuis le 26 juillet 2023, la Région de Niamey a connu une amélioration très appréciable de sa situation sécuritaire. L’état général de notre entité administrative est stable ; sous contrôle absolu et marqué par un ordre et une discipline restaurés grâce aux directives du CNSP. Nous avons mené une offensive implacable contre le petit banditisme et déployé des stratégies robustes pour contrer les menaces terroristes, assurant la protection inébranlable de notre capitale. Le dispositif sécuritaire a été réorganisé pour une efficacité maximale dans la sécurisation et la protection de nos populations. Nous avons créé la brigade des mœurs et réactivé la police sanitaire, essentielles à l’assainissement de notre environnement social. Des opérations de déguerpissement des squatters vivant dans la ceinture verte ont été exécutées pour des impératifs de sécurité et de salubrité, réduisant les zones d’activités illicites. Le leadership du CNSP a profondément impacté la gouvernance : les fonctionnaires sont remis au travail avec rigueur. Le Conseil Régional de Sécurité, sous l’autorité du Gouverneur, est pleinement opérationnel, assurant une coordination sans faille des opérations. La population de Niamey a retrouvé un sentiment de sécurité et de confiance. Bien que des défis sécuritaires persistent à l’échelle nationale, Niamey bénéficie d’une attention particulière, maintenant un niveau de sécurité élevé qui en fait un havre de paix. Les efforts du CNSP pour renforcer la souveraineté du pays sont déterminants. Chaque jour, 21 véhicules du CRS patrouillent les cinq communes. Au premier semestre 2025, la Police de la Ville de Niamey a mené 3.545 patrouilles, 1.294 opérations coup de poing et 59 descentes, interpellant plus de 12.000 personnes. Nous avons démantelé des lieux criminogènes comme SONUCI et la ceinture verte. L’éclairage public et la réhabilitation des voies ont également renforcé la sécurité et fluidifié la circulation. En définitive, la situation sécuritaire de Niamey est transformée. Les actions ciblées, la protection renforcée, la redynamisation des forces de l’ordre, et une administration plus efficace ont collectivement fait de Niamey, une vitrine éclatante du Niger : une ville plus propre, sécurisée, où la population peut vivre et travailler en toute quiétude, avec la certitude que l’Etat veille sur elle avec une vigilance inébranlable.
Quels changements avez-vous relevés dans la vie de la population de votre région et dans son état d’esprit par rapport à la marche du pays ?
Les deux années sous le CNSP ont profondément transformé la vie quotidienne des habitants de Niamey et leur perception de la marche de notre nation. Ces changements ont renforcé la discipline, aiguisé la conscience collective et ravivé le patriotisme. Niamey a changé de visage. Elle est devenue plus propre, plus ordonnée, retrouvant son statut de vitrine du Niger. Cette amélioration est le fruit d’opérations rigoureuses qui ont conduit à un plan de modernisation urbain et à une salubrité accrue. La population est désormais, à l’abri du banditisme urbain, impactant directement leur sécurité et bien-être. Le sentiment de quiétude est revenu. Sur le plan social, une prise de conscience majeure a été observée, particulièrement chez notre jeunesse.
Une lutte implacable est menée contre la prostitution, la consommation de la drogue, de la chicha et la délinquance en milieu urbain et scolaire grâce à un mécanisme de contrôle, de suivi efficaces et à une sensibilisation soutenue. Cette action a permis à nos jeunes de comprendre les dangers et de prendre conscience de leur rôle crucial dans la construction de notre pays. Ce changement de comportement est le résultat d’initiatives de sensibilisation et d’un environnement plus structuré et sécurisé. La Gouvernance a été déterminante dans cette mobilisation, en remettant les fonctionnaires au travail avec rigueur. L’état d’esprit de nos populations est marqué par un regain d’espoir et une confiance inébranlable, Malgré les défis économiques, les habitants de Niamey ont fait preuve d’une résilience exemplaire. Le soutien au leadership actuel est manifeste, car la population perçoit une amélioration tangible de la sécurité et une volonté affirmée de souveraineté nationale. Le complexe d’infériorité a été balayé ; l’Occident n’est plus une référence absolue. Notre peuple a pris conscience qu’il peut compter sur son propre génie pour transformer le pays. Niamey a été à l’avant-garde de cette révolution depuis le 26 juillet 2023. Un nouveau type de citoyen est né, avec pour boussoles, le patriotisme, l’amour et la défense de la patrie. Les mobilisations exceptionnelles lors du sommet de l’AES, des assises nationales, et des cérémonies d’installation du Conseil Consultatif de la Refondation en témoignent. La disponibilité de la population à répondre aux appels du CNSP et du Gouvernement illustre sa foi et son optimisme quant à la marche irréversible du pays vers la vraie souveraineté, le développement et l’indépendance totale. L’espoir est désormais évident. En résumé, la vie de la population de Niamey a été transformée par une sécurité renforcée, une propreté urbaine exemplaire et une prise de conscience collective. L’état d’esprit général est celui d’un soutien inébranlable au commandement actuel et d’un espoir ferme pour l’avenir, bâti sur la dignité retrouvée et la certitude que notre destin est entre nos mains.
Quels sont les principaux acquis à capitaliser notamment dans le cadre du Programme Grande Irrigation ?
«Le Programme Grande Irrigation (PGI) est une vision stratégique majeure pour notre souveraineté alimentaire et notre indépendance économique. A Niamey, les acquis sont tangibles, des victoires concrètes pour l’avenir de notre nation. Un acquis fondamental est la réhabilitation de vastes superficies irriguées, fruit d’un contrat plan pluriannuel entre l’Etat et I’ONAHA. Nous avons réhabilité 320 hectares à Niamey : 54 hectares à Goudel, 64 hectares à Lamordé, 96 hectares à Kirkissoye, et 106 hectares à Saguia Amont. Ces actions réduisent drastiquement nos importations de riz et renforcent notre sécurité alimentaire. Le lancement des travaux de réhabilitation de Saguia Amont, le 23 novembre 2024, est un exemple de notre détermination. Ces travaux sont presque achevés, démontrant notre capacité d’exécution. Ce périmètre de 105,29 hectares augmentera significativement la production de nos exploitants, passant de 6 à 9 tonnes/hectare. La rapidité d’exécution prouve notre efficience opérationnelle. Le PGI vise à réduire notre dépendance aux importations de riz de plus de 83 0/0 à seulement 10-15 0/0 d’ici 2027, avec un total de plus de 39 700 hectares à aménager ou réhabiliter. C’est un plan de bataille clair pour la sécurité alimentaire. Au-delà des chiffres, le programme impacte directement la vie de nos exploitants agricoles. La réhabilitation des périmètres leur offre des infrastructures modernes, augmentant rendements et revenus. Nous sommes satisfaits de l’avancement et nous insistons sur l’importance pour nos exploitants de faire bon usage de ces aménagements pour atteindre la souveraineté alimentaire. Enfin, la prise de conscience de notre jeunesse quant à l’importance de l’agriculture est un acquis inestimable. L’encouragement de nos jeunes à s’investir dans la terre est essentiel pour la pérennité du programme et le développement agricole. Le bilan de I’ONAHA est éloquent : réhabilitation de Saguia Amont pour plus d’un milliard de Francs CFA, mobilisation d’emplois, et une production totale de
13.844,67 tonnes de riz paddy sur 2.667,235 hectares exploités par près de 3.000 exploitants. Notre stratégie porte ses fruits, la souveraineté est en construction».
Quels sont les défis et surtout les espoirs de la population ?
La population de Niamey, à l’instar de l’ensemble du Niger, fait face à des défis complexes, mais nourrit également des espoirs profonds et inébranlables pour l’avenir, renforcés par les dynamiques actuelles sous le leadership éclairé du CNSP. Ces défis sont multidimensionnels, touchant les aspects sécuritaires, socio-économiques et environnementaux, tandis que les espoirs se cristallisent autour de la souveraineté, du développement et d’une meilleure qualité de vie pour tous. Le principal défi demeure la persistance des menaces sécuritaires. Bien que Niamey soit un îlot de paix, les activités des groupes terroristes dans d’autres parties du pays exigent une vigilance constante et des efforts soutenus pour sécuriser l’ensemble de notre territoire national. La guerre contre le terrorisme est un combat de longue haleine, et nous sommes résolus à le mener jusqu’à la victoire finale. Sur le plan socio-économique, le Niger reste confronté à la pauvreté. Malgré les projections de croissance agricole, la pauvreté extrême demeure une réalité. Les sanctions internationales ont eu un impact néfaste sur notre économie, entravant l’aide humanitaire. La forte croissance démographique pose des défis considérables en termes d’accès aux services de base, d’emploi et de ressources. Nous devons construire un avenir où chaque Nigérien aura sa place et sa chance. Les défis environnementaux, tels que les inondations récurrentes, sont également une préoccupation majeure. J’ai pris des dispositions fermes pour y faire face, mais la vulnérabilité de notre ville aux aléas climatiques reste un enjeu important. Nous travaillons sans relâche pour renforcer nos infrastructures et protéger nos concitoyens. A ces défis s’ajoutent l’incivisme, l’occupation anarchique du domaine public, la délinquance juvénile, la mendicité, l’urbanisation galopante, la divagation des animaux et l’insuffisance des infrastructures routières. Autant de fronts sur lesquels nous menons une bataille quotidienne pour l’ordre, la propreté et le bien-être de tous. Malgré ces défis, les espoirs de notre population sont vifs et se fondent sur plusieurs piliers inébranlables. L’un des espoirs majeurs est la consolidation de notre souveraineté nationale. Les actions du CNSP, perçues comme un renforcement de l’indépendance, sont accueillies positivement. Cet espoir de pleine maîtrise de notre destin est un moteur puissant pour l’adhésion aux politiques gouvernementales. Le complexe d’infériorité est parti ; notre peuple a pris conscience qu’il peut compter sur son propre génie pour transformer le pays. Le Programme Grande Irrigation incarne un espoir immense pour l’autosuffisance alimentaire et le développement économique. La perspective de réduire drastiquement les importations de riz et d’augmenter la production agricole locale offre des opportunités concrètes d’amélioration des conditions de vie. L’encouragement de nos jeunes à s’investir dans l’agriculture est également un signe d’espoir pour une diversification économique et une réduction du chômage. C’est la voie vers une prospérité durable. La prise de conscience collective, notamment chez les jeunes, concernant les dangers des stupéfiants et l’importance de leur rôle dans la construction du pays, est un autre motif d’espoir. Cette évolution des mentalités, couplée à une administration plus efficace, crée un environnement propice au progrès social. C’est une jeunesse mobilisée, consciente de ses responsabilités, qui bâtira le Niger de demain. Enfin, le retour progressif de la sécurité et la lutte implacable contre le banditisme à Niamey ont restauré un sentiment de quiétude et de confiance, permettant à la population de se projeter plus sereinement dans l’avenir. Niamey redore son image, et cet effort de transformation est un symbole d’espoir pour l’ensemble du pays. La confiance aux plus hautes autorités, le soutien des populations, l’entente parfaite entre les différentes composantes de la société, et l’extrême jeunesse de notre population sont autant de raisons d’espérer un avenir radieux.
En conclusion, la population de Niamey navigue entre des défis persistants et des espoirs grandissants, alimentés par la quête de souveraineté, les avancées du PGI, une jeunesse plus consciente et un environnement urbain en amélioration. Ces espoirs sont le moteur de la résilience et de la détermination du peuple nigérien, un peuple qui se lève pour construire son destin avec courage et détermination.»
Propos recueillis par
ONEP
a4483.en:
Governor, the CNSP has been in power for two years; what is the general state of your administrative entity, particularly in terms of security?

"Since 26 July 2023, the Niamey Region has seen a very appreciable improvement in its security situation. The general state of our administrative entity is stable, under absolute control and marked by restored order and discipline thanks to the CNSP's directives. We have waged a relentless offensive against petty banditry and deployed robust strategies to counter terrorist threats, ensuring the unshakeable protection of our capital. The security apparatus has been reorganised for maximum effectiveness in securing and protecting our populations. We created the morals brigade and reactivated the sanitary police, essential to cleaning up our social environment. Operations to evict squatters living in the green belt were carried out for security and sanitation imperatives, reducing the areas of illicit activity. The CNSP's leadership has profoundly affected governance: civil servants have been put back to work with rigour. The Regional Security Council, under the Governor's authority, is fully operational, ensuring flawless coordination of operations. The population of Niamey has regained a feeling of security and confidence. Although security challenges persist at the national level, Niamey benefits from particular attention, maintaining a high level of security that makes it a haven of peace. The CNSP's efforts to strengthen the country's sovereignty are decisive. Every day, 21 vehicles of the CRS patrol the five communes. In the first half of 2025, the Niamey City Police carried out 3,545 patrols, 1,294 crackdown operations and 59 raids, arresting more than 12,000 people. We dismantled crime-prone locations such as SONUCI and the green belt. Public lighting and the rehabilitation of roads have also reinforced security and improved traffic flow. In short, Niamey's security situation has been transformed. Targeted actions, reinforced protection, the revitalisation of law enforcement, and a more efficient administration have collectively made Niamey a dazzling showcase of Niger: a cleaner, safer city where the population can live and work in complete peace of mind, with the certainty that the State watches over it with unshakeable vigilance."

What changes have you observed in the life of your region's population and in its state of mind regarding the country's progress?

The two years under the CNSP have profoundly transformed the daily life of Niamey's inhabitants and their perception of our nation's progress. These changes have strengthened discipline, sharpened collective consciousness and revived patriotism. Niamey has changed its face. It has become cleaner, more orderly, regaining its status as Niger's showcase. This improvement is the fruit of rigorous operations that led to an urban modernisation plan and increased cleanliness. The population is now sheltered from urban banditry, which directly affects their security and well-being. The feeling of tranquillity has returned. On the social front, a major awakening has been observed, particularly among our youth.

A relentless fight is being waged against prostitution, drug and shisha consumption, and delinquency in urban and school settings, thanks to an effective mechanism of control and monitoring and to sustained awareness-raising. This action has enabled our young people to understand the dangers and to become aware of their crucial role in building our country. This change of behaviour is the result of awareness-raising initiatives and of a more structured and secure environment. Governance has been decisive in this mobilisation, by putting civil servants back to work with rigour. The state of mind of our populations is marked by renewed hope and unshakeable confidence. Despite economic challenges, the inhabitants of Niamey have shown exemplary resilience. Support for the current leadership is manifest, because the population perceives a tangible improvement in security and an affirmed will for national sovereignty. The inferiority complex has been swept away; the West is no longer an absolute reference. Our people have realised that they can count on their own genius to transform the country. Niamey has been at the forefront of this revolution since 26 July 2023. A new type of citizen has been born, whose compasses are patriotism, love and the defence of the homeland. The exceptional mobilisations during the AES summit, the national consultations, and the ceremonies installing the Consultative Council for Refoundation bear witness to this. The population's readiness to respond to the calls of the CNSP and the Government illustrates its faith and optimism about the country's irreversible march towards true sovereignty, development and total independence. Hope is now evident. In summary, the life of Niamey's population has been transformed by reinforced security, exemplary urban cleanliness and a collective awakening. The general state of mind is one of unshakeable support for the current command and of firm hope for the future, built on regained dignity and the certainty that our destiny is in our own hands.

What are the main achievements to build on, particularly within the framework of the Grand Irrigation Programme?

"The Grand Irrigation Programme (PGI) is a major strategic vision for our food sovereignty and our economic independence. In Niamey, the achievements are tangible, concrete victories for the future of our nation. A fundamental achievement is the rehabilitation of vast irrigated areas, the fruit of a multi-year plan contract between the State and ONAHA. We have rehabilitated 320 hectares in Niamey: 54 hectares at Goudel, 64 hectares at Lamorde, 96 hectares at Kirkissoye, and 106 hectares at Saguia Amont. These actions drastically reduce our rice imports and strengthen our food security. The launch of the rehabilitation works at Saguia Amont, on 23 November 2024, is an example of our determination. These works are almost complete, demonstrating our capacity for execution. This 105.29-hectare perimeter will significantly increase the production of our farmers, rising from 6 to 9 tonnes per hectare. The speed of execution proves our operational efficiency. The PGI aims to reduce our dependence on rice imports from more than 83% to only 10-15% by 2027, with a total of more than 39,700 hectares to be developed or rehabilitated. It is a clear battle plan for food security. Beyond the figures, the programme directly affects the lives of our farmers. The rehabilitation of the perimeters offers them modern infrastructure, increasing yields and incomes. We are satisfied with the progress and we insist on the importance for our farmers of making good use of these developments in order to achieve food sovereignty. Finally, our youth's awareness of the importance of agriculture is an invaluable achievement. Encouraging our young people to invest in the land is essential for the programme's sustainability and for agricultural development. ONAHA's record is eloquent: the rehabilitation of Saguia Amont for more than one billion CFA francs, the mobilisation of jobs, and a total production of 13,844.67 tonnes of paddy rice on 2,667.235 hectares farmed by nearly 3,000 farmers. Our strategy is bearing fruit; sovereignty is under construction."

What are the challenges and above all the hopes of the population?

The population of Niamey, like Niger as a whole, faces complex challenges, but also harbours deep and unshakeable hopes for the future, reinforced by the current dynamics under the enlightened leadership of the CNSP. These challenges are multidimensional, touching on security, socio-economic and environmental aspects, while hopes crystallise around sovereignty, development and a better quality of life for all. The main challenge remains the persistence of security threats. Although Niamey is an island of peace, the activities of terrorist groups in other parts of the country require constant vigilance and sustained efforts to secure our entire national territory. The war against terrorism is a long-haul fight, and we are determined to carry it through to final victory. On the socio-economic front, Niger remains confronted with poverty. Despite projections of agricultural growth, extreme poverty remains a reality. International sanctions have had a harmful impact on our economy, hampering humanitarian aid. Strong demographic growth poses considerable challenges in terms of access to basic services, employment and resources. We must build a future in which every Nigerien will have his place and his chance. Environmental challenges, such as recurrent flooding, are also a major concern. I have taken firm measures to deal with them, but our city's vulnerability to climate hazards remains an important issue. We are working tirelessly to strengthen our infrastructure and protect our fellow citizens. To these challenges are added incivility, the anarchic occupation of public land, juvenile delinquency, begging, galloping urbanisation, the straying of animals and the insufficiency of road infrastructure. So many fronts on which we wage a daily battle for order, cleanliness and the well-being of all. Despite these challenges, our population's hopes are vivid and rest on several unshakeable pillars. One of the major hopes is the consolidation of our national sovereignty. The CNSP's actions, perceived as a strengthening of independence, are welcomed positively. This hope of full mastery of our destiny is a powerful engine for adherence to government policies. The inferiority complex is gone; our people have realised that they can count on their own genius to transform the country. The Grand Irrigation Programme embodies an immense hope for food self-sufficiency and economic development. The prospect of drastically reducing rice imports and increasing local agricultural production offers concrete opportunities to improve living conditions. Encouraging our young people to invest in agriculture is also a sign of hope for economic diversification and a reduction in unemployment. It is the path towards lasting prosperity. The collective awakening, particularly among young people, concerning the dangers of narcotics and the importance of their role in building the country, is another reason for hope. This evolution of mentalities, coupled with a more efficient administration, creates an environment conducive to social progress. It is a mobilised youth, aware of its responsibilities, that will build the Niger of tomorrow. Finally, the gradual return of security and the relentless fight against banditry in Niamey have restored a feeling of tranquillity and confidence, allowing the population to look to the future more serenely. Niamey is restoring its image, and this transformation effort is a symbol of hope for the whole country. Confidence in the highest authorities, the support of the populations, the perfect understanding between the different components of society, and the extreme youth of our population are all reasons to hope for a radiant future.

In conclusion, the population of Niamey navigates between persistent challenges and growing hopes, fuelled by the quest for sovereignty, the advances of the PGI, a more aware youth and an improving urban environment. These hopes are the engine of the resilience and determination of the Nigerien people, a people who are rising to build their destiny with courage and determination."

Interview conducted by
ONEP
